title: U.S. deploys B-1 bomber as attacks on Iran intensify
description: The U.S. military used a B-1 long-range bomber on Tuesday to strike Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets in Iran, U.S. officials said. Why it matters: It was the first time the U.S. conducted a B-1 mission since fighting with Iran resumed 12 days ago. Using B-1 bombers, which can carry two dozen 2,000-lb. bombs or dozens of cruise missiles, signaled a significant escalation and expansion of the U.S. military campaign. The B-1 can fly faster than the speed of sound at low altitudes while carrying the largest bomb load of any type of bomber. Amid a continued U.S. military build up in the region, President Trump is still considering returning to major combat operations against Iran. U.S. and Israeli officials say this could happen within days. Driving the news: The B-1 launched its mission from an airbase in the UK and was spotted on online plane tracking websites. The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) didn't announce the B-1 mission in its statement on Tuesday about the strikes that day. "CENTCOM assets targeted Iranian military operations centers, maritime capabilities, aircraft hangars, drone storage facilities, and military logistics infrastructure to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the statement read. It's unclear what the B-1 attacked and whether the massive mission was more effective than other strikes over the last few days. The U.S. conducted several B-1 missions during Operation Epic Fury, hitting missile bases, command centers, weapons storage facilities and air defense systems. State of play: Despite the expansion of U.S. strikes, the Iranian regime hasn't seemed to change its position on the Strait of Hormuz. And it is still conducting attacks against U.S. bases in the region. Some U.S. defense officials say Iran's military capability around the Strait of Hormuz "is almost nonexistent," but others say Iran is still capable of attacking ships in the area. On Wednesday, President Trump threatened to bomb bridges and power plants, including in Tehran, if Iran attacks more ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by threatening infrastructure in Gulf countries allied with the U.S. Zoom out: Also on Wednesday, Houthi rebels attacked Saudi ships for the first time since they announced a blockade on Saudi ports. A U.S. defense official said the Houthi attacks, after months of almost entirely staying out of the war, could be motivated by Iran. The official said Iran wants to use the Houthis to create a new front in the Red Sea in addition to the Gulf, and to create pressure on another critical international oil shipping route. Several commercial vessels transiting through the Red Sea were seen changing course on Wednesday to avoid passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, fearing Houthi attacks. What to watch: U.S. officials said Qatari mediators are still talking to U.S., Iranian and Omani officials to try to reach a new deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and stop the fighting, according to sources with knowledge. One regional source said Iranian leadership hasn't accepted the latest proposal put forward by the mediators. It's unclear how long Trump will give the diplomatic efforts. "They're getting hit so hard, and they want to make a deal," Trump said in a speech in Georgia Wednesday night. "But I say they're not ready to make a deal because every time they make a deal they want to change it and everything. They're not ready. They will be ready very soon."

title: House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan refers Jack Smith to DOJ over alleged false statement
description: House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) referred former Special Counsel Jack Smith to the Justice Department on Wednesday, alleging he knowingly made false statements during congressional testimony last year. Why it matters: The referral escalates House Republicans' efforts to scrutinize the former special counsel who prosecuted President Trump , even though the Justice Department is not required to act on congressional criminal referrals. Driving the news: "Smith seemingly made willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact that contradict new documents obtained by the Committee from the Department of Justice," Jordan said in a referral to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. "The responses provided by Mr. Smith gave the impression that neither Mr. Smith nor his team had access to the content of members' privileged text messages," said Jordan, referring to members of Congress. "We now know this to be false," he added. "This information calls into question the completeness and accuracy of statements that Mr. Smith made under oath to the Committee regarding his team's access to the content of Members' text messages." The other side: Smith's lawyers, Peter Koski and Lanny Breuer, in a letter to Blanche said the referral was "based on a spurious claim" that Smith had provided false testimony during his eight-hour deposition last December. 'The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement — the letter concedes he did not — but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked," the added. "During his testimony, Mr. Smith provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel. This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law." House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) in a statement called the referral "baseless" and "vindictive," saying Smith told the truth as he gave clear and consistent testimony. "When asked if his subpoena for Members' toll records sought the content of either Member's phone calls or messages, he truthfully replied that they did not. That statement was true when he said it," Raskin said. "It seems Republican Members of Congress are lashing out because they just realized their communications with the White House became presidential records preserved at the National Archives as required by the Presidential Records Act (PRA). This referral deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith's interview." Zoom out: Smith wound down two federal criminal cases he brought against Trump after the president was elected in 2024. Blanche previously led Trump's criminal defense team in those cases. Smith said earlier this year he believed the Trump administration would indict him . Go deeper: 5 key takeaways from Jack Smith's deposition on the Trump probes Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

title: Secret Service threat cases soar 40%
description: Threats against people the U.S. Secret Service protects are up about 40% from a year ago, the agency says, as it prepares for Friday's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner . Why it matters: The increase is stretching Secret Service resources as agents devote more time to investigating threats against senior government officials. Driving the news: "We are seeing a roughly 40% increase from this time compared to last year," Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi tells Axios. "This is roughly 10,000 so far this year and we are a little over halfway through the year," he says. Mental health interventions have increased tenfold from the same period last year, including referrals and both voluntary and involuntary commitments involving people encountered during its protective mission, he says. The big picture: News of the surge comes ahead of Friday's White House Correspondents' Dinner. The original dinner was derailed after shots were fired in the D.C. building where President Trump was due to address the White House correspondents in April. A 31-year-old California man, Cole Tomas Allen , faces charges including attempting to assassinate the president. Context: In addition to protecting the president, the Secret Service is tasked with protecting Supreme Court justices, cabinet members, former presidents, presidential candidates and foreign leaders visiting the U.S. Go deeper: Timeline of shootings, threats against Trump over the years

That statement was true when he said it," Raskin said. "It seems Republican Members of Congress are lashing out because they just realized their communications with the White House became presidential records preserved at the National Archives as required by the Presidential Records Act (PRA). This referral deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith's interview." Zoom out: Smith wound down two federal criminal cases he brought against Trump after the president was elected in 2024. Blanche previously led Trump's criminal defense team in those cases. Smith said earlier this year he believed the Trump administration would indict him . Go deeper: 5 key takeaways from Jack Smith's deposition on the Trump probes Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

title: Secret Service threat cases soar 40%
description: Threats against people the U.S. Secret Service protects are up about 40% from a year ago, the agency says, as it prepares for Friday's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner . Why it matters: The increase is stretching Secret Service resources as agents devote more time to investigating threats against senior government officials. Driving the news: "We are seeing a roughly 40% increase from this time compared to last year," Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi tells Axios. "This is roughly 10,000 so far this year and we are a little over halfway through the year," he says. Mental health interventions have increased tenfold from the same period last year, including referrals and both voluntary and involuntary commitments involving people encountered during its protective mission, he says. The big picture: News of the surge comes ahead of Friday's White House Correspondents' Dinner. The original dinner was derailed after shots were fired in the D.C. building where President Trump was due to address the White House correspondents in April. A 31-year-old California man, Cole Tomas Allen , faces charges including attempting to assassinate the president. Context: In addition to protecting the president, the Secret Service is tasked with protecting Supreme Court justices, cabinet members, former presidents, presidential candidates and foreign leaders visiting the U.S. Go deeper: Timeline of shootings, threats against Trump over the years

title: Tesla's push into AI and robotics is proving costly
description: Tesla's massive investments in humanoid robots , self-driving cars and AI chips are hurting profits, but the company says it'll all pay off down the line. Why it matters: CEO Elon Musk indicated he's "never been more optimistic about the future," but acknowledged the investments could lead to uneven results. Zoom in: Tesla revenue jumped on record vehicle deliveries in the second quarter, but the company saw a significant dip in operating profit because of its heavy spending on R&D. Tesla plans to spend more than $25 billion on capital investments this year, and that spending rate will grow over the the next two or three years, CFO Vaibhav Taneja told investors and analysts on a call late Wednesday. Additionally, Tesla plans to borrow as much as $30 billion to accelerate its investments in robotaxis, Optimus robots, semiconductors, solar manufacturing and AI compute infrastructure, he said. "We're investing a lot in growing the core business and really preparing for the future," Musk said on the call. "So this is a massive capex year, but I'm confident that all the things that we're investing in will yield incredible returns — really, maybe the best capex returns that we've ever seen." By the numbers: Tesla reported Q2 revenue of $28 billion, up 23% year over year. Net income was $1.1 billion, down 5% compared to a year ago, and essentially flat with the last three quarters. Operating margin fell to just 1.4%, compared to 4.1% a year ago. State of play: Tesla began production of its driverless Cybercab in Texas during the quarter, but Musk said its Robotaxi service is rolling out cautiously to ensure safety. Tesla Semi remains on track for production later this year at a new factory in Nevada, but Musk said autonomous trucking is not a priority until next year. The company said it's making progress to expand battery pack manufacturing capacity, which it called "the main limiting factor to near-term vehicle production volume increase." Tesla tore out assembly lines for its discontinued Model S and X cars at its Fremont, Calif., factory and expects Optimus humanoid robot production to begin there later this year. Musk acknowledged that scaling Optimus production will be difficult. "This is going to be the hardest product to scale manufacturing that we've ever made at Tesla, because everything on the robot is new." The bottom line: Tesla's focus is always over the horizon.

title: Senate feeling good about avoiding pre-election shutdown
description: Senators on both sides of the aisle are quietly hopeful about avoiding a third government shutdown this year. Why it matters: Time is short, patience is wearing thin and neither party wants to head into the campaign's final sprint under the cloud of a funding lapse. "People understand that it would be helpful to have a [continuing resolution] that extends beyond the election," Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) told Axios. "So it doesn't get all bound up in partisan discussions around the elections." "I just think everybody's trying to give ourselves room to find a bipartisan agreement, and we are not there yet," Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) told Axios. Asked whether the vibes were positive, Schatz replied: "Not negative." Republicans were even more optimistic about a bipartisan CR. "Perhaps we can get ours passed, and then when the House comes back the last week of August, they can pass it there," Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said. "I don't think there's going to be much controversy there, unless the Democrats change their minds." State of play: The House passed a short-term spending bill late Tuesday night. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) will essentially ignore it. For now. The same fate likely awaits the budget resolution Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) narrowly pushed through Wednesday afternoon on a 216-214 vote. The intrigue: House Republicans are still steaming over Thune's decision to declare, in advance, that he won't take up reconciliation until the government is funded. "He's the leader of the Senate. I think it's a mistake to hold up such an important piece of legislation," House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios. But his new Senate counterpart, Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.), appears far more comfortable with Thune's timeline and sequencing. "With [Senate Appropriations Chair] Susan [Collins] apparently showing progress toward a CR — even talking about a defense supplemental in that agreement — that would, to a certain extent, negate having to do one," Johnson said, referring to a separate reconciliation package. What to watch: There's no guarantee a major news event won't derail bipartisan funding talks, just as Medicaid cuts and the ICE shootings did earlier this year. President Trump's escalation of the conflict with Iran is already complicating defense spending negotiations, with Democrats largely opposed and Republicans split over the scope of additional funding. Any effort to attach supplemental defense money tied to Iran to the CR could make the vote significantly more difficult. Zoom out: The CR is only one item on the Senate's crowded pre-recess agenda. FISA Section 702 remains lapsed, leaving the intelligence community without a key surveillance authority. The Senate also must take another run at the National Defense Authorization Act after the bill stalled this month. Thune also wants to reserve time for the CLARITY Act , but both sides acknowledge that more work needs to be done to find 60 Senate votes for the cryptocurrency bill. There is also building pressure for Thune to bring a Russia sanctions package to the floor, especially after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who had pushed hard for the bill's passage. And leadership is trying to clear a backlog of nominations, including Jay Clayton to serve as director of national intelligence and Todd Blanche to serve as attorney general. The bottom line: On Tuesday, Thune slyly suggested that he was prepared to use a reconciliation package to fund the government along party lines -- if needed. He may not have to act on that threat if the bipartisan Senate progress continues.

title: "The DCCC is not God": Tensions erupt over House Democrats' failed primary meddling
description: House Democrats are demanding a reckoning after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spent over $500,000 backing a candidate in Arizona who is on track to lose her primary. Why it matters: This is the third time in 2026 the House Democratic campaign arm has tried and failed to intervene in a party primary, leading some lawmakers to argue that its money is better spent elsewhere. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), a top DCCC dues payer , said the party should be "rationing our resources to win general elections," calling for "a conversation about ... what the involvement in primaries looks like." "That's $100,000 that I put in," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) said of her dues, arguing that the DCCC "shouldn't be spending this money" on primaries. Driving the news: Former Arizona state Rep. Amish Shah led former TV journalist Marlene Galán-Woods in the Democratic primary in Arizona's 1st district by roughly seven percentage points as of Wednesday evening. With 87% of the votes reporting Galán-Woods "still has a chance" but "I would much rather be Shah than her," one House Democrat who has followed the race closely told Axios. The DCCC ran a $514,000 joint ad buy with the Galán-Woods campaign after endorsing her as part of its "Red to Blue" program in June, according to AdImpact. Zoom out : This latest loss for the DCCC comes after it fell short in California's 22nd district , where progressive activist Randy Villegas won in an upset over more moderate state Assembly member Jasmeet Bains in June. Later that month, DCCC-endorsed state Sen. Joe Baldacci lost to progressive rival Matt Dunlap in Maine's 2nd district. The DCCC ran roughly $250,000 in joint ad buys with Bains and Baldacci, according to AdImpact and other ad data viewed by Axios. What they're saying: "Can you imagine if we'd put that $800,000 in the general election so we can win in November," said Ramirez, adding, "I would recommend that we just don't engage in primaries." "I personally don't think we should be investing against Democrats when we've got a big battleground," Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), who represents swing-district House Democrats in leadership, told Axios. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-Ariz.) told Axios: "When we have caucus-funded organizations that are paid through dues, we should not be picking winners and losers among Democrats." Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said he wants the DCCC to endorse Dunlap and other progressive candidates like Tom Periello, telling Axios: "We've got to really look not through a traditional prism but at candidates who can build a grassroots organization and speak to the times." What we're hearing: Behind the scenes, some of the DCCC's top dues payers are even more livid. "People are mad," a senior House Democrat told Axios. Said one House Democrat who has paid all their dues: "I would prefer to see the dollars that I invest spent on candidates who won their Democratic primaries rather than have the DCCC inject themselves." "The DCCC is not god," The lawmaker added. "They cannot dictate outcomes. There needs to be an acknowledgement that there's a limit to the ability of the DCCC to choose what it considers to be the perfect candidate." Another House Democrat who is also paid up in full told Axios the DCCC "shouldn't be taking a position in a primary unless everybody agrees, and I'm not aware anyone was consulted." The other side: "We move onto the general. We're going to win that general election, and we're going to win the majority; that's an incredibly important district to do it," Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) told Axios. Stanton, a co-chair of the DCCC's frontline program, vowed to "make sure we are not outspent in that race" come November. "I have all the confidence in [DCCC Chair] Suzan DelBene to make the decisions she feels appropriate to take back the majority," Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) told Axios. "At the end of the day, Democrats are united in our shared goal to flip the House and make life affordable for everyday Americans," said DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton.

title: New Pipelines Set To Ease Permian Natural Gas Glut
description: The regional price of natural gas produced in the Permian, the top U.S. oil basin, was negative for most of the first half of the year. Rising associated gas output from oil-targeting wells has had nowhere to go. Producers had to either flare the gas, within allowed limits, or pay to get rid of what many Permian players see as an undesirable by-product of the valuable crude. For years, the key constraint to local gas prices has been the insufficient pipeline takeaway capacity, which hasn’t grown in lockstep with the soaring gas production…
